column4: The source reads the surah's back as a camel carrying another's load; this ayah depicts deniers carrying their own burdens on their backs at the Hour (يَحْمِلُونَ أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ), reversing useful cargo into the consequence of one's deeds.

The source's pack camel can bear someone else's physical load; this ayah draws the boundary that no soul bears another's moral burden, then says return is to the Lord, distinguishing carried cargo from personal accountability.

Like 6:164, this ayah says no bearer carries another's burden and that return is to the Lord; beside the source's load-bearing camel, it marks moral responsibility as a load that cannot be handed to a mount.
The source's camel bears provisions and people along the road; this ayah reverses that image with creatures that carry no provision of their own, whom God still sustains along with people.
The source turns the surah into a caravan journey; this ayah names Quraysh's regular winter and summer journeys, an explicit parallel of recurring travel by caravan.
The source's mount leads to remembrance of the Lord; after 106:2 names Quraysh's journeys, this ayah directs them to worship the Lord of the House, setting devotion as the caravan's response.

The source presents animal travel as mercy and provision; this closing ayah says the Lord feeds Quraysh against hunger and secures them from fear, completing the journey-and-worship sequence of 106:2–3.
This ayah names Quraysh's settled security (إِيلَافِ قُرَيْشٍ); 106:2 specifies the seasonal journeys whose reliable rhythm gives the source's recurring caravan travel a close historical parallel.
The source's camels stop for water and pasture; this ayah pairs drinkable rainwater with plants in which livestock graze (فِيهِ تُسِيمُونَ), directly supplying both parts of that stop.
The source names pasture as where camels remain; this ayah commands people to eat and pasture their livestock (وَارْعَوْا أَنْعَامَكُمْ), following 20:53's paths and rain with the animal's grazing.
The source's caravan needs pasture after water; this ayah describes rain brought to barren land producing crops eaten by people's livestock, repeating that provision cycle.

The source's camel is a workable mount even when difficult to train; this ayah uses a camel entering a needle's eye (الْجَمَلُ فِي سَمِّ الْخِيَاطِ) as an impossible threshold, reversing the animal's role as a means of passage.
The source's route ends by turning toward the Lord; Abraham says he is migrating to his Lord (إِنِّي مُهَاجِرٌ إِلَىٰ رَبِّي), making a real departure and its divine destination explicit.
The source makes “to your Lord” the caravan's destination; Abraham says he is going to his Lord and expects guidance, joining travel, divine direction, and arrival.
The source's caravan bears loads for its journey; this pilgrimage ayah tells travelers to take provisions and calls God-consciousness the best provision, applying the load image to the Hajj road.

The source says that after one task is finished, effort and desire turn toward God; this Hajj ayah describes departing Arafat, seeking bounty from the Lord, and remembering Him at the sacred landmark.

The source's animal journey arrives at a sacred destination; this ayah protects sacrificial offerings and garlanded animals while people travel toward the Sacred House seeking God's bounty and approval.

The source's camel completes a road to a place of rest; this ayah says the sacrificial offering was held back from reaching its place (مَعْكُوفًا أَنْ يَبْلُغَ مَحِلَّهُ), showing the animal's route interrupted before arrival.
The source contrasts two camel paces, easy and difficult; this ayah says people have been shown two paths (النَّجْدَيْنِ), opening a moral choice later pictured as an uphill pass.
Where the source has sustained travel and exertion, this ayah says the person did not attempt the difficult pass (الْعَقَبَةَ); 90:12–17 explain the hard ascent as costly acts of care and faith.
This ayah asks what the steep pass is, naming a difficult route; 90:13–17 supply its concrete acts, giving the source's hard road a moral counterpart.
The source's difficult road requires exertion; this ayah names freeing a slave as one act on the steep pass, while 90:14–17 complete the costly path.
This ayah adds feeding on a day of hunger to the steep pass; it connects the source's loaded journey to provision for the hungry, with 90:15–17 completing the passage.
This ayah specifies feeding an orphan who is a near relative as one part of the steep pass, making the source's road-work an act of care; 90:16–17 continue the path.
This ayah names feeding a destitute person in misery on the steep pass; the source's strenuous route is thus paralleled by costly care, completed by the faith and patience of 90:17.
This ayah completes the steep-pass sequence with faith, patience, and mercy, giving the source's effort toward the Lord a moral destination after the concrete acts in 90:13–16.
This ayah identifies those who took the steep pass as people of the right; it supplies the outcome of the difficult path described in 90:11–17, beside the source's road toward its Lord.

The source dictionary's ظ ه ر branch uses noon for the camels' daily watering; this ayah names the noon privacy/rest period (مِنَ الظَّهِيرَةِ), giving the camel's water stop a human midday counterpart.

The source's وَضَعَ dictionary branches describe lowering or setting a mount down; this ayah says a mother carries her child in hardship and lays him down in hardship, shifting the heavy-load image from a beast's back to gestation and birth.

The source dictionary branch of ص د ر describes camels departing from water; this ayah uses يَصْدُرُ for people dispersing to see their deeds, a different setting but a specific echo of leaving a stopping place for what follows.
The source's ر ف ع branch describes a camel's raised pace; this ayah uses the same root for God raising believers in rank, a different kind of elevation that qualifies the physical gait reading.

The source develops ر غ ب as a wide-striding horse and as desire directed to the Lord; this ayah uses the root for turning away from Abraham's way, a specific reversal of the source's directed desire, though the sense is distinct.
